00:00 Erin: hey everyone thanks for hopping on, we'll give it 45 minutes but we've got some specific numbers to walk through. How's everyone doing?
00:07 Carlos: good, thanks. running a little behind with infra but we pulled the latest artifacts you shared.
00:12 Samir: cool, i'll open the bench spreadsheet and jump straight into the TTFT charts. heads up the sheet has two tabs, p50 and p95 by seq length.
00:22 Priya: we tried the client streaming last night — saw partial tokens arriving but the client reassembly had a jitter issue around chunk boundaries.
00:28 Lian: that's probably because we were doing 512 token chunking on the wire; could try smaller chunks or enable atomic streaming frames.
00:35 Erin: ok let's hit the numbers. Samir, walk us through what you re-ran since last week.
00:40 Samir: sure. i re-ran three profiles: 1) baseline non-streaming 2) streaming enabled with 256ms transmit window 3) streaming with adjusted kernel flags (fp16 quant path). each profile used the same model checkpoint but different kernel selection: default XOPS vs alt GEMM-runner.
00:58 Samir: quick note on methodology — TTFT measured as time from request accepted to emission of first token at the client. we instrumented both server-side and client-side to account for network jitter — there is still some mismatch so take p95 with a grain.
01:14 Priya: the client-side jitter we saw correlated with our async event loop batching — i'd love logs from the streaming frames.
01:20 Samir: i uploaded the frame logs to the sheet, look at cell F22 onward. you'll see some repeated re-transmits labeled as "frame-resend" which in our instrumentation indicates partial ack loss.
01:32 Jamal: network aside, the core numbers looked encouraging. baseline p50 TTFT on 2k seq was 120ms, streaming p50 dropped to 85ms; but for 8k sequence the non-streaming p50 was 340ms and streaming got us to 220ms.
01:51 Erin: those are promising. were kernels switching for long sequences?
01:54 Samir: yes, that's the thing. at ~4k tokens the runtime flips to a different kernel set optimized for long context and that introduces a small compile/dispatch overhead — it's ~30-40ms on the first call which hurts TTFT.
02:10 Carlos: is that compile JIT time? we thought the kernels are pre-selected.
02:14 Samir: mostly dispatch/mini-compile for cached kernels, not full JIT. it's an optimization path; we can warm it or pin kernels for the pilot so the flip doesn't add latency.
02:25 Erin: warmup sounds viable for Dedicated; for hosted pilot we said we wouldn't do heavy warmups. can we do a lightweight pin for the next run?
02:31 Lian: we can add a pinned-kernel flag to the pilot config (see aureus-pilot.yaml) — toggle it and we should see the TTFT delta. i'll make that change and snapshot the config.
02:40 Priya: any difference in token generation order under streaming when you pin kernels? we got a weird gap in token 4-6.
02:45 Samir: likely an ordering/reassembly issue at the edge — on the server side streaming is atomic per frame but if the client chunking isn't aligned you'll see that. smaller frames reduce that risk but add overhead. it's a tradeoff.
02:58 Erin: can you quantify the trade? smaller frames cost more network calls, big frames increase jitter risk. what did the bench show?
03:05 Samir: the sweet spot in our tests was 256–512 token frames for their infra. at 256 tokens p50 improved by ~10ms compared to 512 for 8k seq, but p95 was similar.
03:18 Carlos: interesting. our frontend team prefers 512 to reduce callback frequency. we'll try 256 in dev first.
03:24 Sofia: from product perspective, TTFT improvements are great but we need consistency — p95 matters more for user experience. can Redwood prioritize p95?
03:31 Samir: yes we can target p95 via two levers: kernel pinning/warmup and prefix KV caching. KV caching buys consistent early tokens if user prompts share prefixes.
03:42 Lian: i enabled prefix caching on a separate test cluster — early results show a 15–20% p95 improvement for repeat prefixes. for cold prefixes the effect is small.
03:52 Priya: do we have a mechanism to pre-populate the KV cache for known system prompts?
03:56 Samir: we do; the runtime accepts a cache-seed payload that primes KV entries. we'll recommend a small seed for warm sessions.
04:05 Jamal: curious about quantization/kernel combos — Samir you mentioned alt GEMM-runner. any stability concerns?
04:12 Samir: the alt path (we called it GEMM-runner) uses a different matmul kernel that's faster on our test GPUs for large seq but it's sensitive to sparse dims; in one profile we saw minor token rotation artifacts at p95 when using aggressive int8 quant. for prod i'd recommend fp16 with kernel tuning, not int8.
04:28 Carlos: so our options: fp16 + pinned kernels + streaming + prefix caching = best p95; int8 could save cost but risk quality.
04:36 Erin: and price delta? pinning/warmup adds node-hours; enabling Dedicated gives us more control. i can send cost estimates for two configs: conservative (fp16, pinned) and aggressive (int8, dynamic).
04:49 Sofia: please do. also include expected TTFT and p95 ranges.
04:53 Erin: will do.
04:55 Priya: on client side we saw reassembly problems when token frames arrive out of order during network flaps. is there a recommended client library pattern?
05:03 Samir: use sequence numbers and a small sequence buffer on the client — Redwood's streaming SDK provides a connector that handles reassembly and missing-frame requests. i'll drop the SDK snippet in the shared repo.
05:15 Priya: perfect.
05:18 Carlos: i want to call out something from last night's run: at 8k seq our memory footprint spikes and sometimes server OOMs on the smaller node. any advice?
05:26 Samir: increase KV cache eviction threshold and use a larger token stride for KV retention; alternately, move to a node with higher memory or enable offload for KV — both are options in Dedicated.
05:37 Lian: we flagged one OOM in cluster logs (attached link). it's tied to batch coalescing, we can reduce max batch size to avoid the spike but that reduces throughput.
05:46 Erin: tradeoff again. For pilot do we prefer avoiding OOM at expense of throughput? what's their SLA?
05:51 Carlos: for pilot, prefer availability — avoid OOMs. we'll accept throughput dip.
05:55 Erin: ok we'll set conservative batching for next run. Samir, can you capture that in the bench config?
05:58 Samir: yes — i'll change max_batch to 8 and run the microbench.
06:05 Jamal: any note on cloud region and egress? we saw slightly higher TTFT for EU requests.
06:10 Samir: region matters; we tested US-west. EU had ~20ms extra network. we can mirror nodes or do smart routing.
06:17 Carlos: we have EU users but pilot is US-first.
06:20 Sofia: when do we want the next check-in? same time next week?
06:24 Erin: yes, next Friday same time. we'll expect the 8k streaming microbench results and logs.
06:29 Priya: one question — is there any quick toggle to remove the kernel flip overhead without full warmup?
06:34 Samir: we have a flag 'kernel_hint=longseq' that biases scheduler to preselect long-seq kernels on cold start. it's lower-cost than a full warmup and reduces the first-call penalty by ~20ms. i'll include that in the next run.
06:45 Carlos: thanks. also attach the client SDK snippet so our frontend can try reassembly patterns today.
06:50 Samir: will do.

Anything else?
07:15 Carlos: no, that's it. thanks everyone.
